name: Protected culture
summary: Growing berries under plastic or glass, often in substrate — a production-system choice that changes season, disease pressure, and capital, not a variety name.
what_is_it: Protected culture covers high tunnels, greenhouses, and related structures that modify rain, temperature, and sometimes daylength. Many commercial strawberry programs now use table-top or trough substrate rather than in-ground plasticulture; blueberry and raspberry are also grown in pots or substrate under cover in some regions. The plant still has the same biology (chill, fruiting habit, flavor chemistry); the structure changes what weather the plant sees and how water, fertilizer, and pests are managed.
why_it_matters: Winter production, rain-free picking, and 'glasshouse berry' competitive claims are usually protected-culture stories. Capital cost, energy, and labor differ from open field. A variety that works in a tunnel may still fail in open-field chill or rain.
how_evaluated: Described by structure type, substrate vs soil, heating, and harvest calendar — not by a single instrument reading. Yield-per-square-meter figures from one greenhouse cannot be copied onto a field acreage claim.
what_affects_it: Climate, energy cost, nursery plant type, pollination (often bumblebees in closed houses), and whether the crop is strawberry, raspberry, or blueberry. IPM still applies; some pests increase under cover.
how_to_interpret: Do not treat 'greenhouse' or 'tunnel' as proof of premium flavor or of a company's market share. Geography still matters. Pair with winter production, chill hours (the plant may still need a dormancy strategy), and harvest methods. Absence of a tunnel in a source is not proof the farm is open-field.
